items.prompt: Which term describes noticing and naming your own emotions as they happen?

options.label: Self-awareness
Social influence
Self-regulation
Empathy

rubric: Self-awareness is recognising your own feelings as they occur.
Self-regulation is managing emotions, not just noticing them.

items.prompt: What does empathy mean in emotional intelligence?

options.label: Hiding your feelings from other people
Solving another person's problems for them
Understanding and sharing what another person feels
Agreeing with everything another person says

rubric: Empathy is understanding another person's feelings.
Agreeing or fixing is not the definition of empathy.

items.prompt: Which is a common skill of self-regulation?

options.label: Acting on the first impulse
Ignoring feelings completely
Telling others how to feel
Pausing and breathing before responding

rubric: Pausing helps manage strong emotions.
Ignoring or acting on impulse is not regulation.

items.prompt: Which of these is a nonverbal cue that can reveal emotion?

options.label: Email subject line
Facial expression
Job title
Meeting agenda

rubric: Facial expressions are nonverbal emotional cues.
The others are not body signals of emotion.

items.prompt: What is the term for the ability to read other people's emotions and respond to them well?

options.label: Self-awareness
Social awareness
Self-motivation
Self-control

rubric: Social awareness is reading others' emotions.
The other terms focus on the self.

items.prompt: Which of the following are commonly listed components of emotional intelligence? Select all that apply.

options.label: Self-regulation
Empathy
Memorising facts quickly
Self-awareness

rubric: Self-awareness, empathy and self-regulation are core components.
Fast memorising is a cognitive skill, not an EQ component.

items.prompt: Dana feels her face get hot and her heart race after a harsh comment in a meeting. She silently thinks, "I am feeling angry right now." Which emotional intelligence skill is Dana using?

options.label: Avoidance
Self-awareness
Empathy
Social influence

rubric: Naming her own feeling is self-awareness.
She has not yet acted to manage it or read others.

items.prompt: Why is it useful to name an emotion, such as "I feel frustrated," before reacting?

options.label: It makes the feeling disappear permanently
It proves that the other person is wrong
It creates distance so you can choose a response
It shows others you should not be challenged

rubric: Naming emotions helps you pause and choose.
Naming does not erase feelings or assign blame.

items.prompt: A colleague says "I'm fine" in a flat voice, looking down, with crossed arms. What is the best interpretation?

options.label: They are bored and want to leave
They are definitely fine because they said so
Words and body language may not match, so they may be upset
They are angry at you personally

rubric: Mismatched cues suggest something may be wrong.
Jumping to certain conclusions is unsupported.

items.prompt: Which best explains the difference between empathy and sympathy?

options.label: Empathy is pity; sympathy is understanding
They mean exactly the same thing
Empathy is feeling with someone; sympathy is feeling for them
Empathy needs agreement; sympathy does not

rubric: Empathy shares the feeling; sympathy is concern from outside.
Empathy does not require agreement.

items.prompt: Which response shows good self-regulation when you receive critical feedback?

options.label: Defend yourself right away to stop the criticism
Take a breath, listen, then ask a clarifying question
Say nothing and resent it afterwards
Point out the other person's own mistakes

rubric: Calm listening and clarifying shows regulation.
Defending, resenting or counterattacking are reactive.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes self-regulation?

options.label: Avoiding any situation that causes stress
Managing how you express and respond to feelings
Letting feelings decide your actions immediately
Suppressing all emotions so you never feel them

rubric: Regulation is managing responses, not eliminating feelings.
Suppression and avoidance are common misconceptions.

items.prompt: Which of these are examples of active listening that show empathy? Select all that apply.

options.label: Interrupting with your own similar story
Paraphrasing what the person said
Giving full attention without checking your phone
Reflecting their feeling, such as "That sounds stressful"

rubric: Paraphrasing, reflecting and attention show empathy.
Interrupting with your story shifts focus away from them.

items.prompt: A teammate named Sam seems quiet and snaps at a question after learning a project was cancelled. Priya thinks, "Sam is probably disappointed, so the sharp tone may not be about me." What is Priya doing?

options.label: Reading Sam's emotion and not taking the tone personally
Ignoring Sam's feelings to stay productive
Deciding that Sam is rude and should apologise
Hiding her own feelings to avoid conflict

rubric: She interprets the cause of Sam's behaviour with empathy.
Other options assume rudeness or ignore the emotion.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes self-awareness in emotional intelligence?

options.label: Hiding your feelings so that other people are never affected by them
Noticing what you feel as it happens and how it shapes your choices
Knowing what other people feel without needing them to tell you
Staying positive all day so that your mood never changes at work

rubric: Self-awareness is recognising your own emotions and their effect on behaviour.
Distractors confuse it with suppression, mind-reading, or forced positivity.

items.prompt: What most clearly separates empathy from sympathy?

options.label: Empathy requires agreeing with the person; sympathy allows you to disagree
Empathy tries to see how the person feels from their view; sympathy feels sorry for them
Empathy means feeling the identical emotion; sympathy means giving advice
Empathy is for friends and family; sympathy is meant for the workplace

rubric: Empathy involves understanding another's perspective; sympathy is concern from the outside.
Distractors invent rules about identical feelings, settings, or agreement.

items.prompt: Why does silently naming a feeling, such as "I'm anxious right now", often help you regulate it?

options.label: It creates a little distance, which makes the feeling easier to manage
It removes the feeling completely, so you stop experiencing it
It proves the feeling is correct, so others will have to accept it
It makes the feeling stronger so you can act on it faster

rubric: Labelling creates distance and reduces the feeling's intensity.
Distractors claim it amplifies, validates, or eliminates the emotion.

items.prompt: Which example shows self-regulation rather than emotional suppression?

options.label: Venting right away so that the feeling cannot build up inside you
Feeling irritated, taking a breath, then stating your concern calmly
Saying nothing and pretending you feel fine while still seething inside
Avoiding the person who upset you so that you never feel it again

rubric: Self-regulation acknowledges the emotion and chooses a calm response.
Distractors are suppression, impulsive venting, or avoidance.

items.prompt: After you give feedback, a colleague crosses his arms and answers in short phrases. What is the most reasonable reading?

options.label: Body language is unreliable, so only his spoken words should count
He may be uncomfortable, so a gentle check-in is better than assuming
He is bored, so you should wrap up the conversation quickly
He definitely disagrees, so you should defend your feedback more firmly

rubric: Cues suggest possible discomfort and should be checked, not assumed.
Distractors jump to a firm conclusion or dismiss nonverbal cues entirely.

items.prompt: Which of these are signs of strong emotional self-awareness? Select all that apply.

options.label: Never feeling anger or frustration at work
Knowing which situations tend to trigger stress for you
Naming a feeling before deciding how to respond
Recognising that being tired makes you more irritable
Believing your feelings always give an accurate view of the facts

rubric: Self-aware people link feelings to causes, name them, and know their triggers.
Distractors assume feelings are always accurate or that anger never occurs.

items.prompt: In a team meeting, Priya is cut off twice by a colleague. She then stops contributing and looks down at her notes. Afterwards, when asked, she says "It's fine." What does her behaviour most likely signal?

options.label: She is relaxed, since quiet people rarely feel upset by interruptions
She has nothing more to add, so her words match what she feels
She dislikes the topic and would like the group to drop it
She may feel dismissed and is withdrawing, though her words say otherwise

rubric: Withdrawal after interruptions suggests feeling dismissed despite 'It's fine'.
Distractors take words at face value or attribute the behaviour to personality.

items.prompt: At 4:55pm a client sends an angry email that makes you furious. Which action best applies self-regulation?

options.label: Reply immediately so the client sees you are responsive
Step away briefly, then reply once your reaction has settled
Forward it to your team with a comment about the client's tone
Ignore it entirely so that the conflict fades by itself

rubric: Pausing lets the emotional reaction settle before a considered reply.
Distractors are impulsive reactions, venting, or avoidance.

items.prompt: A teammate who missed a deadline tells you, "I'm so stressed." Which first response best applies empathy?

options.label: "That sounds stressful. What has been the hardest part for you?"
"Everyone is stressed right now, so you just have to push through."
"Don't worry, deadlines slip all the time and it's not a big deal."
"Here is a five-step plan that will fix your schedule."

rubric: Acknowledging the feeling and inviting them to talk shows empathy.
Distractors minimise, jump to fixing, or dismiss the feeling.

items.prompt: Your heart is racing ten minutes before a presentation. Which technique best calms your body?

options.label: Breathe in for four counts and out for six, repeating for a minute
Tell yourself firmly to stop feeling nervous right now
Speed-read your slides again to burn off the nerves
Drink a strong coffee so that you feel more alert

rubric: Slow breathing with a longer exhale lowers physical arousal.
Distractors suppress the feeling or add stimulation and pressure.

items.prompt: A coworker keeps sending reports late. Which wording best uses an "I" statement to raise it?

options.label: "People around here are starting to think you don't care."
"I get worried when reports arrive late because I can't finish mine. Can we agree a time?"
"Why can't you just be on time like everyone else does?"
"You are always late and it is ruining everything I do."

rubric: An 'I' statement names your feeling and the impact, then proposes a solution.
Distractors blame, generalise, or use others as pressure.

items.prompt: A friend says, "I didn't get the job, and I worked so hard for it." Which reply best reflects their feeling?

options.label: "Maybe you should have prepared in a different way."
"You sound really disappointed after putting so much into it."
"You'll find something better soon, so try to cheer up."
"At least you still have your current job to rely on."

rubric: Reflecting the emotion shows you understood it.
Distractors offer false cheer, criticism, or silver linings.

items.prompt: You feel anger rising during a tense meeting. Which actions apply self-regulation? Select all that apply.

options.label: Stay silent and agree with everything to avoid conflict
Pause and take a slow breath before you speak
Ask for a short break if the feeling stays strong
Interrupt now to make your point before you forget it
Raise your concern calmly with specific examples once settled

rubric: Pausing, taking a break, and calm expression are regulation strategies.
Interrupting is impulsive; silent agreement is suppression.

items.prompt: A customer is shouting at a service rep about a late delivery. The rep feels defensiveness and tension rising. Which response best applies emotional intelligence?

options.label: Raise their own volume a little so the customer knows they are serious
Notice the tension, slow their breathing, acknowledge the frustration, then explain next steps
Explain company policy first so the customer sees it was not their fault
Offer a full refund immediately so that the call ends quickly

rubric: Regulating oneself and acknowledging feelings calms the exchange before problem-solving.
Distractors escalate, get defensive, or rush to end the conflict.

items.prompt: A manager's curt email leaves you with a racing heart and tight jaw. Which sequence best applies self-regulation before you reply?

options.label: Name the feeling, pause until the arousal drops, then answer the content
Reply right away while the point is fresh, so you sound confident
Vent to coworkers first, then reply once they agree with you
Push the feeling down and send a flat, neutral reply immediately

rubric: Labelling the emotion and pausing lowers arousal so the reply can be deliberate.
Immediate replies and suppression leave the emotion in control; venting amplifies it.

items.prompt: After your proposal is heavily edited in a meeting, a teammate goes quiet and crosses their arms. Which next step best applies empathy?

options.label: Tell them in the meeting that the edits were nothing personal
Ask privately and openly how they see the changes, then listen
Send a group note praising everyone's flexibility with the edits
Assume they are fine and move on to the next agenda item

rubric: A private open question invites their view and shows you noticed.
Reassuring them publicly or ignoring the cues skips finding out what they feel.

items.prompt: A client cancels at the last minute and you feel insulted. Which response is an example of cognitive reappraisal?

options.label: Checking your phone and focusing on other tasks until it fades
Considering that the client may be handling a crisis unrelated to you
Telling yourself the feeling is silly and refusing to think about it
Complaining about the client to a colleague until you feel better

rubric: Reappraisal changes the interpretation of the event, which changes the emotion.
The other options are suppression, distraction and venting.

items.prompt: You must give feedback to a colleague who gets defensive when criticised. Which approach best applies emotional intelligence?

options.label: Describe one specific behaviour and its impact, then ask for their view
Say you are disappointed in them and wait for their reaction
Open with a long list of their faults so nothing is left unsaid
Soften it so much that the actual issue is never stated clearly

rubric: Specific behaviour plus impact and an invitation reduces threat and keeps the message clear.
Piling on, vagueness or judgments of the person raise defensiveness or hide the point.

items.prompt: A customer, angry after a week without service, is shouting at you. Which opening line best applies emotion labelling to de-escalate?

options.label: "Our policy says outages take up to ten days to resolve."
"I understand completely, but shouting won't make it faster."
"A week without service is frustrating; let's get it fixed now."
"Please calm down so that I can help you with this."

rubric: Naming the feeling and its cause shows it was heard and moves toward action.
Telling them to calm down, citing policy or scolding invalidates the emotion.

items.prompt: During a tense salary negotiation, which actions apply self-regulation? Select all that apply.

options.label: Agreeing quickly to the terms so the discomfort ends sooner
Treating the counter-offer as information rather than a personal insult
Hiding every sign of emotion so the other side learns nothing
Asking for a short break when you notice your tension rising

rubric: Taking a break and reframing both manage the emotion while staying engaged.
Caving to escape discomfort and total concealment are avoidance and suppression, not regulation.

items.prompt: You manage a team member whose output has dropped. In your one-to-one she becomes tearful when you mention the missed targets. You planned to review the numbers for the full half hour. What should you do next?

options.label: Tell her you understand and that everyone struggles sometimes
Acknowledge the emotion, offer a pause, and ask what would help
Continue through the numbers so the meeting stays professional
Cut the meeting short and reschedule without any explanation

rubric: Acknowledging her emotion and asking what helps shows empathy while keeping the issue open.
Pressing on ignores her state; abrupt ending or generic reassurance avoids real engagement.

items.prompt: Dana snaps at a colleague's routine question right after a meeting where her work was overlooked. Later she says, "I don't know why I overreacted." What is the best analysis?

options.label: She is simply rude and lacks any capacity for empathy
Her colleague's question was objectively provocative in tone
She has weak impulse control that shows up in every situation
Emotion from the earlier slight was displaced onto an unrelated trigger

rubric: The disproportionate reaction fits displaced feeling that she had not recognised.
The other options blame traits or the colleague instead of tracing the cause.

items.prompt: A colleague says "I'm fine" in a flat tone and avoids eye contact, though she is normally chatty. What is the most defensible analysis?

options.label: Avoiding eye contact shows dishonesty and a reason to distrust her
She is definitely upset, because body language never lies
The mismatch with her usual baseline is a cue to check in, not proof
Her words are what count, so she should be taken at face value

rubric: Cues compared to a person's baseline are hypotheses that call for a gentle inquiry.
Treating nonverbal signals as certain, or ignoring them, both misread emotional data.

items.prompt: An upset coworker is told "Just calm down," and becomes louder. Which explanation best accounts for the escalation?

options.label: The coworker lacks the intelligence to follow a reasonable request
Raising their voice shows that they were never really upset
The phrase was too short, so a longer instruction would have worked
The phrase dismisses the feeling, so they feel unheard and push harder

rubric: Invalidating an emotion signals it was not heard, which tends to raise arousal.
The other options blame the person or the length rather than the effect of invalidation.

items.prompt: A leader is warm and always understands her team's stress, yet deadlines keep slipping. Which analysis best identifies the flaw?

options.label: Her team is probably unmotivated, whatever her style may be
She treats understanding as a reason to waive expectations and accountability
She is too empathic, so empathy should be reduced in leaders
Warmth is a poor leadership trait that causes missed deadlines

rubric: Empathy does not require lowering standards; the gap is in holding people accountable.
The other options blame empathy itself or the team without examining how the leader responds.

items.prompt: An employee reads nearly every neutral email from colleagues as hostile and replies defensively. Which underlying gap best explains this pattern?

options.label: Too much empathy with senders who write briefly
Poor typing skills that make her replies seem blunt
A need for more detailed emails from her colleagues
Little awareness of how her own expectations colour her reading of others

rubric: Consistent hostile attribution points to a self-awareness gap about her interpretive filter.
The other options misplace the cause in typing, excess empathy or the senders.

items.prompt: Which observations suggest a person is reacting emotionally rather than disagreeing in a considered way? Select all that apply.

options.label: Asking a clarifying question before stating an objection
Responding within seconds using absolutes such as "always" and "never"
Changing position after seeing new data
Being unable to restate the other person's point when asked

rubric: Instant absolutes and inability to restate the other view signal narrowed, reactive thinking.
Clarifying questions and updating on evidence indicate considered engagement.

items.prompt: Two team members, Ana and Ben, are in conflict. Ana says Ben is dismissive in meetings; Ben says Ana is oversensitive and takes everything personally. Each describes the other's character, not specific events. Which analysis best explains the pattern?

options.label: Ben is deliberately undermining Ana and should be disciplined
Ana is simply too sensitive, as Ben says, and should adapt
The two are a poor match and should be moved to separate teams
Each reads the other's behaviour through their own emotions, so they argue about traits

rubric: Both attribute traits instead of describing events, showing emotional filters on each side; the next step is separate fact-based accounts.
Siding with one person or separating them jumps to a conclusion before diagnosing the cause.

items.prompt: In a meeting, a teammate says "No problem, go ahead" about your schedule change, but his jaw tightens and he stops contributing. What is the soundest analysis?

options.label: The mismatch between his words and behaviour signals an unspoken concern that should be checked, not assumed.
Silence after agreement always means passive aggression, so you should document it for later.
His words are the reliable data, so he has accepted the change and the silence is just fatigue.
The tightened jaw proves he is angry at you personally, so you should confront the hostility directly.

rubric: Incongruence between words and nonverbal cues is a prompt to check, not a verdict.
Distractors either ignore the cues or over-read them as proof of intent.

items.prompt: After harsh criticism, Dana fires off a cutting email within two minutes and regrets it later. Which breakdown best explains this?

options.label: She had no pause between trigger and response, so the reaction drove her action before appraisal.
She did not know professional email norms, so a style guide would have prevented the reply.
She was too empathetic toward the critic, so she absorbed the hostility and returned it.
She felt too little emotion, so she failed to take the critique seriously enough to reflect.

rubric: The failure is in self-regulation: no gap for appraisal between stimulus and action.
Distractors blame knowledge, too little emotion, or excess empathy rather than the missing pause.

items.prompt: A manager feels a distressed colleague's pain so intensely that he starts avoiding her and cannot offer help. Which analysis is most accurate?

options.label: His shared feeling, left unregulated, has become personal distress that pulls him away from helping.
He is suppressing his emotion, which reliably increases a person's capacity to help others.
He lacks cognitive empathy, since he cannot recognise that she is upset.
He shows healthy empathic concern, so avoiding her is a form of respecting her privacy.

rubric: Unregulated affective empathy can become personal distress and withdrawal rather than concern.
Distractors misread him as unable to recognise her state or praise avoidance.

items.prompt: After bad news, Ana hides her reaction by suppression while Ben reinterprets the news as a chance to re-plan. Which comparison is best supported?

options.label: Reappraisal changes the meaning early so the emotion is dampened, while suppression hides expression but arousal persists.
Both strategies work identically once the person looks calm, since observers cannot see the difference.
Suppression lowers both outward expression and internal arousal, so it is the more efficient strategy.
Reappraisal ignores the facts of the event, so it works only by denying that the news was bad.

rubric: Reappraisal acts on appraisal; suppression changes only the expression, leaving physiological arousal.
Distractors credit suppression with internal calming or call reappraisal denial.

items.prompt: Why does distinguishing "disappointed" from "ashamed", instead of just feeling "bad", improve emotional regulation at work?

options.label: Naming the emotion lets you rule it out as irrelevant, so decisions rest only on facts.
Distinct labels point to different appraisals and needs, such as re-planning for disappointment or repair for shame.
Precise words make the feeling weaker automatically, whatever you then decide to do about it.
Specific labels mainly help you describe feelings to others, with little effect on your own choices.

rubric: Emotional granularity links a feeling to its likely cause and fitting response.
Distractors treat labelling as automatic dampening, mere communication, or dismissal.

items.prompt: A usually upbeat colleague has become terse, misses small details and skips lunch. Which analyses are sound? Select all that apply.

options.label: The change from her own baseline is more informative than any single behaviour taken alone.
Her terse replies show she has a grievance with whoever spoke to her last.
Several causes, such as workload or non-work stress, remain plausible until she is asked.
Skipping lunch confirms burnout, so the right step is to report it to HR.

rubric: Baseline comparison and holding multiple hypotheses are the sound reading of cues.
Distractors jump to a single cause or escalate on thin evidence.

items.prompt: Marcus, a manager, notices he turns curt whenever junior analyst Lee questions his estimates. On reflection he recalls a former boss who dismissed his estimates in front of others. Lee's questions are polite and data-based. Which analysis best explains Marcus's reaction?

options.label: Marcus is too empathetic toward Lee and is deflecting the discomfort of correcting him.
Lee's challenges are subtle disrespect that Marcus is correctly detecting.
Marcus's curtness shows low confidence in the numbers, so he should simply recheck them.
A past association is being triggered by a similar cue, so the reaction exceeds what Lee's behaviour warrants.

rubric: The reaction is a trigger from a past experience, disproportionate to the present cue.
Distractors attribute the reaction to Lee's intent or to unrelated causes.

items.prompt: In a one-to-one, an employee begins crying after your feedback. Criteria: preserve her dignity, keep the feedback usable, avoid dismissing the emotion. Which response best meets them?

options.label: Withdraw the feedback and reassure her it did not matter, so she is not upset any further.
Continue through all the feedback quickly, since prolonging the meeting would make it more painful.
Acknowledge the emotion, offer a short pause, then confirm which points to revisit together.
End the meeting and reschedule without comment, so she can compose herself privately.

rubric: Acknowledging emotion and pausing keeps dignity while the feedback stays intact.
Distractors rush, retract, or avoid, each failing one of the criteria.

items.prompt: Ten minutes before a key presentation, your heart is racing. Criteria: act quickly, reduce physiological arousal, and not undermine performance. Which strategy is best?

options.label: Rehearse every worst-case failure to desensitise yourself before you go on.
Check your phone so the feeling fades while your attention is elsewhere.
Slow, exhale-weighted breathing, then reframe the arousal as readiness to perform.
Tell yourself firmly to calm down and not feel nervous, to remove the anxiety.

rubric: Breathing targets arousal quickly and reappraisal channels it into performance.
Distractors use thought suppression, rumination on failure, or distraction.

items.prompt: An angry customer says an order was lost twice. Criteria: de-escalate, show understanding, move to a solution. Which opening is best?

options.label: Offer a quick apology and a discount before they finish, to end the conflict fast.
Match the customer's intensity of tone, to show you take the complaint seriously.
Explain the policy reasons thoroughly first, so the customer understands how this happened.
Name the frustration, then state the specific next step you will take right now.

rubric: Naming the feeling and giving a concrete step de-escalates and moves to resolution.
Distractors defend, mirror anger, or buy off the customer before listening.

items.prompt: A colleague says, "I'm highly emotionally intelligent because I never lose my cool." Judged against what the skills include, what is the best critique?

options.label: Calm may reflect suppression or detachment, and says little about reading others or knowing your own state.
The claim cannot be assessed, because emotional skills are not observable in any behaviour.
The claim holds, since outward calm is the most direct evidence of emotional skill.
The claim fails because emotionally intelligent people should visibly express every emotion they feel.

rubric: EI covers self-awareness, reading others and regulation, not just looking calm.
Distractors equate calm with skill, demand full expression, or deny observability.

items.prompt: A report was submitted late. Criteria: keep accountability, keep people reporting problems candidly, and protect the relationship. Which manager response best meets them?

options.label: Express strong disappointment once, so the standard is unmistakable, then move on.
Review the cause in the team meeting so that everyone learns from it.
Ask what happened and what support is needed, then agree a fix in a curious tone.
Say nothing this time to protect morale, and watch whether it happens again.

rubric: Curious inquiry plus an agreed fix keeps accountability without punishing candour.
Distractors use shame, avoidance or public exposure, which erode safety or accountability.

items.prompt: You are angry after a colleague's remark and could raise it now or tomorrow. Which are sound reasons, given the goal of a productive conversation, to wait until tomorrow? Select all that apply.

options.label: Waiting always lowers the other person's anger, whatever the issue.
High arousal still narrows your thinking and makes a hostile tone more likely.
You cannot yet separate what was said from your interpretation of it.
The issue will probably resolve itself if you ignore it for long enough.

rubric: Waiting is justified when arousal and unchecked interpretation would distort the talk.
Distractors assume delay always helps or that avoidance resolves conflict.

items.prompt: Nadia learns that a peer took credit for her work. She is furious, and in an hour both attend a client meeting. Criteria: protect the client relationship, avoid acting on raw anger, and still address the issue. Which plan is best?

options.label: Suppress the matter entirely, since raising it would damage your standing with the team.
Confront him just before the meeting, so the issue is out and cannot leak into your manner.
Regulate briefly now, stay professional in the meeting, and schedule a private talk afterwards.
Signal displeasure subtly in the meeting, so he knows without a direct scene.

rubric: Regulating first and deferring a private conversation meets all three criteria.
Distractors act on anger, avoid the issue, or use passive aggression in front of the client.

items.prompt: A manager must stay composed through a high-stakes negotiation tomorrow. Criteria: keep performance steady, lower physiological arousal, avoid hiding the feeling at the table. Which preparation is best?

options.label: Reappraise the meeting as a solvable challenge beforehand, which lowers arousal without hiding feelings later
Vent to colleagues just before walking in, because fully expressing emotion always discharges it completely
Suppress outward signs of anxiety during the talks, which keeps composure and removes the need to process it
Avoid thinking about the meeting until it starts, since attending to feelings only amplifies them further

rubric: Reappraisal before the event changes the emotion's meaning and lowers arousal without costly concealment.
Suppression and avoidance leave arousal high; venting does not reliably discharge emotion.

items.prompt: A director says: 'High emotional intelligence means staying upbeat and agreeable so nobody feels uncomfortable.' Which critique is soundest?

options.label: It is wrong, because EQ concerns only reading others and has no bearing on how you manage your expression
It is correct, because agreeableness is the main behavioural marker that emotional intelligence measures in leaders
It is mostly correct, but upbeat displays should be limited to formal meetings and periods of high stress
It confuses EQ with suppression; skilled use includes naming discomfort and disagreeing constructively

rubric: EQ means accurately perceiving and using emotion, including productive disagreement, not enforced positivity.
Distractors equate EQ with agreeableness or ignore self-management.

items.prompt: A manager must deliver layoff news to several people this week. Criteria: convey real understanding, keep making sound decisions, avoid personal burnout. Which empathy approach best meets them?

options.label: Rotate which affected people you speak to so that you only feel strongly about a small few of them
Understand each person's perspective and show concern, without absorbing their distress as your own
Stay emotionally detached and stick to policy language so decisions are never clouded by any feeling
Fully mirror each person's distress so they feel completely understood, accepting the personal cost of it

rubric: Cognitive empathy plus empathic concern conveys understanding while protecting judgement and wellbeing.
Mirroring distress risks burnout; detachment fails the understanding criterion.

items.prompt: In a 360 review, a manager rates herself 4.5/5 on listening while peers average 2.5/5. Which way of judging the gap is best?

options.label: Treat the gap as a possible blind spot and ask peers for specific recent examples before concluding
Average the two scores to 3.5 and treat that figure as her most accurate level of listening skill
Discount the peer scores as rater bias, since peers rarely observe all of her listening in full
Trust her self-rating, since only she knows her real intent when she is listening to other people

rubric: A self-other gap is data about blind spots; concrete examples let her test it.
Distractors defend self-perception or average away informative disagreement.

items.prompt: Training tells staff to judge colleagues' feelings from facial expressions alone. The teams span cultures and personalities. Which assessment is best?

options.label: Trust the first impression, since quick intuitive reads are consistently more accurate than checking
Rely on expressions, because basic emotions are displayed identically across all people and situations
Treat expressions as one cue, tested against context and the person's baseline, then check by asking
Ignore expressions entirely, since only what people say in words can be a valid source of information

rubric: Expressions are ambiguous cues; context, baseline and verification make reading more accurate.
Distractors assume universality, discard useful cues, or trust unchecked intuition.

items.prompt: A course teaches that reading micro-expressions lets managers detect lying by employees. Which are sound criticisms of this approach? Select all that apply.

options.label: Confident misreads can wrongly damage trust with employees who are being honest
Reading emotions is unrelated to workplace relationships, so it need not be taught
Micro-expressions never occur, so the method has no observable basis at all
Without a person's baseline and context, such readings cannot be interpreted reliably
Brief expressions are ambiguous, since the same look can signal stress or fear rather than deception

rubric: Ambiguity, cost of misreads and missing baseline are real limits on deception detection.
Denying that expressions exist, or that emotion-reading matters, overstates the critique.

items.prompt: Sam, normally chatty, has been curt since being passed over for promotion. You manage Sam and have a one-on-one tomorrow. You want to support Sam, preserve trust, and avoid presuming the cause. Which opening is best?

options.label: 'I know you're upset about the promotion, so let's talk through why the decision went the way it did.'
'Your tone has affected the team lately, so I need you to be more positive in meetings from now on.'
'I've noticed you seem quieter lately, and I'm curious how things are going, if you'd like to share.'
'Let's keep this strictly to project status today, since personal matters are better kept out of work.'

rubric: A tentative observation with an open invitation respects autonomy and avoids assuming the cause.
Naming the cause presumes; demanding positivity or avoiding feelings damages trust.

items.prompt: Design a routine for someone who snaps when interrupted in meetings. Constraints: usable within five seconds, replaces snapping, keeps the person assertive. Which fits?

options.label: Name the feeling silently, take one slow breath, then calmly ask to finish your point
Match the interrupter's volume to regain the floor quickly, then apologise for the tone afterwards
Count to ten silently, then say nothing so the conflict never escalates into open disagreement at all
Suppress the irritation completely, then raise the matter with the interrupter in writing after the meeting

rubric: Labelling, a breath and a specific request fit the time limit and keep assertiveness.
Counting to ten is too slow and passive; suppression and volume-matching fail the constraints.

items.prompt: Design a 30-minute debrief after a team conflict. Constraints: no blame, everyone is heard, ends with commitments. Which structure meets all three?

options.label: Review the facts only, skip feelings, and email action items afterwards for people to accept silently
Open discussion with no structure, so people raise whatever feels most important in the moment to them
Agree the facts, have each person share impact and needs in turn, then agree specific changes together
Each person lists what others did wrong, then the manager rules on who must change their behaviour

rubric: A sequenced facts, impact, needs and commitments format is blame-free, inclusive and ends in action.
Other options assign blame, lack structure, or skip the emotional and commitment steps.

items.prompt: Design a 6-week plan for an engineer who rates her empathy highly while colleagues disagree. Constraints: uses outside data, is measurable, carries low risk. Which fits?

options.label: Log triggers and reactions daily, and every two weeks compare them with peer feedback on specific behaviours
Take a self-report empathy questionnaire every week and aim to raise her own score by the end of the plan
Ask her manager to rate her once at the end, and adopt whichever behaviours the manager lists for her
Read widely about empathy for six weeks and write a reflective summary of what she would do differently

rubric: Repeated logs compared with external behavioural feedback are measurable, outside-sourced and low-risk.
Self-report scores, reading, or a single rating lack outside data or measurable change.

items.prompt: Design a response to burnout in a customer support team driven by emotional labour. Constraints: service quality stays, approach is evidence-based, cost is low. Which fits?

options.label: Give agents bonuses for fewer complaints so they feel motivated to hide stress and keep going on calls
Coach agents to take the customer's view rather than fake feelings, plus recovery breaks and peer debriefs
Cut call volume sharply for every agent indefinitely, accepting slower service as the necessary price for it
Require agents to keep smiling with scripted warmth, supported by stress-management slides in annual training

rubric: Deep acting, recovery time and peer debriefs address emotional labour cheaply while keeping service.
Surface acting worsens burnout; volume cuts break quality; bonuses encourage hiding stress.

items.prompt: An EQ programme teaches staff to name their emotions and use breathing to calm down, then ends. What is most clearly missing from this design?

options.label: A test scoring how many emotion words staff can list, since vocabulary is the core of the skill
More breathing techniques, since calm alone is sufficient for good interpersonal outcomes in any situation
Instruction to avoid expressing emotions at work, so that calm becomes the default for everyone
A step for choosing a behaviour from the read of the situation and checking its effect afterwards

rubric: Awareness and calming must lead to a chosen action and a feedback check to affect relationships.
Distractors add more of the same, measure vocabulary, or promote suppression.

items.prompt: Design a script for a client angry about a missed deadline. Constraints: acknowledge their emotion, preserve their dignity, concede nothing you cannot deliver. Which elements belong in it? Select all that apply.

options.label: State what you can do next and by when
Name the specific frustration without implying you agree with every claim
Tell them to calm down so the conversation can become rational
Promise the original terms to end the anger quickly
Acknowledge the impact on their plans in respectful language

rubric: Acknowledging feeling separately from agreement, plus a concrete next step, meets all constraints.
Telling someone to calm down dismisses them; promising undeliverable terms breaks the no-concession constraint.

items.prompt: You must announce a reorganisation to an anxious team. Legal limits what you can say about roles, and you feel anxious too. Constraints: stay steady, be honest, address the team's fear. Which plan fits?

options.label: Delay the announcement until you feel no anxiety whatsoever, so your delivery projects complete certainty to the whole team
Rehearse and reframe your nerves beforehand, name likely worries, state what is known and unknown with a next-update date, offer small follow-ups
Share your own guesses about role changes to build trust, since openness matters more to the team than the legal limits do
Read a neutral approved script without mentioning feelings at all, so that nothing said can be taken as promising or alarming anyone

rubric: Pre-regulation, naming concerns and honest known/unknown framing satisfy steadiness, honesty and fear.
Scripts ignoring emotion, speculation breaching limits, and waiting for zero anxiety each fail a constraint.
